title: the ranges ahead
hook: a young man comes home from his studies proud, and his father asks one question he can't answer
carry: ask about what you think you know

segments.voice: Yesterday: darshana, a way of seeing. One mountain, many valleys, and the schools taught side by side.

A son walks back into his father's house after years away at study. He has learned the Vedas. He carries himself like someone who has finished. The Chandogya Upanishad doesn't flatter him: it says he came home proud, thinking himself learned. His father, Uddalaka, asks one question, and the son, Shvetaketu, who knows so much, has no idea what his father means. Year two walked through this scene. It comes back today, one day before the year closes, as the doorway to the last of the ranges ahead: the great sayings.
screen: `HOME FROM STUDY, PROUD.` → `ONE QUESTION FROM HIS FATHER.` → `NO IDEA WHAT HE MEANS.`

segments.voice: Here's the question, in paraphrase: did you ask for that teaching by which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought becomes thought, the unknown becomes known? Shvetaketu says, sir, what kind of teaching is that? So his father gives him a picture. By knowing one lump of clay, you know everything made of clay. The pot, the cup, the lamp: the difference is a name, a way of speaking. What's real is the clay. Then comes the line that makes the scene. Shvetaketu says, in effect: surely my teachers didn't know this, or why wouldn't they have told me? Teach me, sir. He came home finished. One question later, he's a beginner again, asking to be taught. What follows in the Upanishad is a long teaching, and inside it is a short phrase his father says to him: tat tvam asi, that you are. Tradition counts it among the great sayings, and the path plans to give those sayings a week each, near the end of the fifth year. So why this scene at the end of year three? It's tempting to walk back in the door like Shvetaketu, carrying what you've learned like a finished thing: the Mahabharata, the saints, the teachers, the practices. They are real, and they count. But the ranges ahead are full of teachings not yet heard. In the Upanishad, the real teaching starts only once he says teach me, sir.
screen: `THE TEACHING THAT MAKES THE UNHEARD HEARD.` · `ONE LUMP OF CLAY.` · `TEACH ME, SIR.` · `TAT TVAM ASI, AHEAD ON THE PATH.` · then, large: `A BEGINNER AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing this path taught you this year, a story, a line, a practice, and hold it up like the lump of clay. Don't recite it; ask what's underneath it that you haven't heard yet, then set it down and simply breathe, with nothing finished. If you pray, you can bring the words teach me to God in your own way; if you don't, let the question stay with you through the sit.
Shvetaketu. The student who came home proud and thinking himself learned, and left a beginner again, ahead on the ranges toward the great sayings.
Your line: ask about what you think you know. The proud graduate became a beginner, and that was the start. One day left in year three.

howItsDone: The dialogue between Uddalaka and Shvetaketu in the Chandogya Upanishad is taught in Vedanta as the setting of the saying tat tvam asi, and some Hindu teachers retell it as a lesson in a student's humility.

chat.says: Why does Shvetaketu's story matter if he'd already learned the Vedas?
options: Because one question showed him there was more to learn, and he asked to be taught.
Because his father scolded him for skipping his Vedic studies years ago.
Because he went back to school and studied the Vedas all over again.

notes: Day 6 (last) of 'the ranges ahead' (1054–1059). Angle: year five's great sayings, through the Shvetaketu homecoming (Chandogya 6.1). Days 1054–1056 were not on disk when written; check for overlap. The Chandogya was read in year two (days 332–359), so this scene may have been told there; the angle here is the end-of-year homecoming.

Editor pass: cut the invented 'watches him for a while'; 'glad to be' (not in the text) became 'asking to be taught', and the screen's large line now reads 'a beginner again'; 'says to him more than once' cut to 'says to him' (the count is not in the cited verse); 'it's one of the great sayings' attributed to tradition; 'near the top of the fifth year' corrected to 'near the end' (weeks 45–50); howItsDone 'often' softened.

Audit (2026-10-01): the homecoming and the clay were already taught on days 339-340 (year two), but the hook presented them as new ('something stranger'); the hook now says year two walked through this scene and that it returns as the doorway to the great sayings. 'The Upanishad treats teach me, sir, as a better place to stand than I know' (an evaluative claim the text doesn't make) became 'the real teaching starts only once he says teach me, sir'. 'A week each' for the great sayings follows the outline; confirm against y5.
The length of Shvetaketu's study (the text gives his age and years) is deliberately not stated.
Chandogya 6.1.2–3 (proud, thinking himself learned; the ādeśa), 6.1.4 (clay, vācārambhaṇaṃ vikāro nāmadheyam), and 6.1.7 (my teachers must not have known; teach me, sir) paraphrased. Confirm.
'Says to him more than once': tat tvam asi recurs at the end of 6.8–6.16; the exact count is not stated. Confirm.
'Near the top of the fifth year' reflects the path outline (year five, weeks 45–50); not yet written or reviewed.
